claims.text: Pre-depositing a thin, uniform nickel layer on the tungsten phase will overcome phase separation in a W–Cu composite.
Pre-depositing a thin, uniform nickel layer on the tungsten phase will suppress interfacial void formation in a W–Cu composite.
The nickel treatment will enhance thermal conductivity under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to W-based plasma-facing/Cu-based cooling joints.
The initial composite consists of tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten ligaments embedded in a copper matrix.
Untreated W–Cu develops phase separation under high heat flux and irradiation.
Untreated W–Cu develops interfacial voids under high heat flux and irradiation.
The intervention is to deposit a thin, conformal nickel interlayer on tungsten surfaces before consolidation or sintering.
High heat flux and irradiation are relevant service exposures for tungsten-based plasma-facing materials.
Processing will produce a continuous, nanometer-scale nickel layer between tungsten and copper.
The nickel layer enhances wetting between tungsten and copper.
The nickel layer promotes formation of a graded interphase between tungsten and copper.
The proposed graded interphase reduces interfacial mismatch.
The nickel layer slows deleterious atomic diffusion at the W–Cu interface.
Improved wetting, reduced mismatch, and slower diffusion suppress phase separation and void nucleation.
The modified interface maintains continuous thermal pathways during thermal and irradiation stress.
Nickel-coated samples will have a more homogeneous interface and fewer voids than untreated samples under identical conditions.
Nickel-coated samples will have higher thermal conductivity than untreated samples under identical heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
Effectiveness requires a uniformly deposited nickel layer of nanometer-scale thickness.
The effectiveness of the nickel layer under extreme irradiation or atypical processing conditions is uncertain.
